title: LoKO: Low-Rank Kalman Optimizer for Online Fine-Tuning of Large Models

raw.stage1:
### Purpose
The contribution's purpose is to provide a second-order alternative to gradient-based optimizers for online fine-tuning of large models, cast as an optimal filtering/state-estimation problem. Paper [2] compares backpropagation with the Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) for training neural networks, explicitly positioning EKF as a second-order alternative to gradient-based methods. Paper [19] interprets optimization as a stochastic filtering problem, aligning with the state-estimation framing. Both papers share the same problem-class objective: leveraging second-order methods (EKF) for neural network optimization. Thus, the purpose is **covered**.

### Mechanism
The mechanism combines LoRA's low-rank decomposition with the Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) to estimate only the low-rank trainable parameters online. Paper [3] introduces a low-rank EKF for online learning of neural networks, using a decomposition of the posterior precision matrix to reduce computational cost. Paper [23] also proposes a low-rank Kalman filter under model uncertainty, demonstrating compatibility with low-rank systems. Both papers substantively overlap with the mechanism's core primitive: combining low-rank decomposition with EKF for efficient parameter estimation. Thus, the mechanism is **covered**.

### Evaluation
The evaluation reports convergence with fewer iterations and comparable or better performance than commonly used optimizers with LoRA. Paper [8] evaluates LoRA's convergence and performance in parameter-efficient fine-tuning, while Paper [2] compares EKF and backpropagation in terms of convergence speed and effectiveness. Both papers use similar evaluation designs: comparing convergence and performance metrics across optimizers. The evaluation design is **covered**.

### Domain
The domain is parameter-efficient fine-tuning/optimization for large models. Paper [8] explicitly addresses LoRA for fine-tuning large-scale models, and Paper [18] discusses adaptive freezing in LoRA-based fine-tuning. Both papers operate in the same general application area of parameter-efficient fine-tuning for large models. The domain is **covered**.

## Purpose

The purpose is: "Provide a second-order alternative to gradient-based optimizers for online fine-tuning of large models, cast as an optimal filtering/state-estimation problem."

Paper [2] compares EKF as a "second-order training method which can be applied to the problem of learning neural network parameters." Paper [19] (KOALA) proposes "to consider the loss as a noisy observation with respect to some reference optimum" — casting optimization as a filtering/state-estimation problem for neural network training. Paper [6] explores EKF as "a viable alternative" to first-order algorithms for training deep neural networks. However, none of these specifically target *fine-tuning large models* as the objective — they target training from scratch. The purpose of providing a second-order optimizer *for fine-tuning large models* (not training from scratch) is partially covered by the LoRA-related papers, but those use first-order methods. The closest is [19] which casts optimization as state estimation for neural networks, and [2]/[6] which use EKF as second-order alternative. At the problem-class level — "second-order/filtering alternative to gradient optimizers for neural network parameter learning" — papers [2], [6], [19] cover this. The "large model fine-tuning" specificity belongs to domain.

## Mechanism

The mechanism is: "Combine LoRA's low-rank decomposition with EKF so that only the small set of low-rank trainable parameters is estimated online (LoRA-Kalman compatibility)."

Paper [3] proposes "an efficient online approximate Bayesian inference algorithm... based on the extended Kalman filter (EKF), but uses a novel low-rank plus diagonal decomposition of the posterior precision matrix." This combines EKF with low-rank structure for online neural network learning — very close. However, [3]'s low-rank is on the *precision matrix* (covariance approximation), not on the *parameter space* via LoRA decomposition. Paper [7] addresses "low-rank systems" with Kalman filtering using Kronecker product decomposition. Paper [5] uses decoupled EKF for factorization models (which are inherently low-rank). The key primitive here is: restrict EKF to operate only on LoRA's low-rank parameters. Paper [3] is the closest — it combines EKF with low-rank decomposition for online neural network learning — but the low-rank structure in [3] is applied to the covariance/precision matrix, not to the parameter space itself via LoRA. No prior paper explicitly combines LoRA (low-rank parameter reparameterization) with EKF for large transformer fine-tuning. This appears genuinely absent.

## Evaluation

The evaluation design: "Converges with fewer iterations and yields better/comparable performance than commonly used optimizers with LoRA."

This is a standard comparative evaluation design — comparing convergence speed and final performance against baseline optimizers. Paper [2] explicitly compares EKF vs backpropagation "with respect to their effectiveness and speed of convergence." Paper [6] compares EKF against first-order algorithms for image classification. Paper [27] reviews second-order vs first-order convergence comparisons. The evaluation design (compare second-order method vs first-order baselines on convergence and accuracy) is well-covered by [2] and [6].

## Domain

The domain is: "Parameter-efficient fine-tuning / optimization for large models."

Papers [8], [12], [14], [18], [20], [21], [24], [25], [26], [29] all work in parameter-efficient fine-tuning of large models using LoRA variants. This domain is clearly covered.

## Purpose: Reduce computational complexity of Kalman iterations and make observation-noise estimation robust.

The purpose has two parts: (1) reducing computational complexity of Kalman filter iterations, and (2) robust estimation of observation noise covariance R. Paper [9] (Kalman Optimizer) applies Kalman filtering to DNN optimization and discusses computational efficiency. Paper [34] addresses computational complexity of Kalman filter via inverse-free methods. Papers [1], [4], [13], [17], [26], [29] address adaptive/robust noise covariance estimation. However, the specific combined purpose of reducing complexity *within a LoRA/PEFT optimization context* while also making R estimation robust is partially covered: [34] covers complexity reduction, and [13]/[17]/[29] cover robust noise covariance estimation. Paper [9] specifically targets Kalman-based neural network optimization efficiency. The purpose at the problem-class level (reduce KF complexity + robust R estimation) is covered by [34] (complexity) and [13]/[17] (robust R estimation).

## Mechanism: Diagonal approximation of P (quadratic→linear complexity) + EMA for R estimation + Taylor-based refinement of R, integrated into LoRA.

**Diagonal approximation of P**: Paper [32] uses diagonal approximation of covariance in spectral ensemble Kalman filters. Paper [34] uses diagonal approximation of innovation covariance matrix for inverse-free KF. These cover the diagonal covariance approximation primitive.

**EMA for noise covariance estimation**: Paper [7] explicitly uses exponential moving average to estimate process noise covariance via innovation term covariance. Paper [28] uses EMA in an extended Kalman filter context. Paper [10] analyzes the equivalence between EMA and Kalman filter. These cover the EMA-for-covariance-estimation primitive.

**Integration into LoRA**: No prior paper combines these within LoRA specifically, but the individual primitives (diagonal P approximation, EMA for R) are covered. The Taylor-based refinement of R is not clearly covered by any prior paper. However, the core mechanism primitives (diagonal P + EMA for R) are covered by [32]/[34] and [7]/[28] respectively.

The combination integrated into LoRA is new as a whole, but the individual primitives are covered. Since the question asks whether any prior paper contains a substantively equivalent element, the diagonal approximation is in [32]/[34], and EMA for noise estimation is in [7]. The Taylor refinement is not clearly covered. Given the mechanism is a combination, I'll cite the closest matches.

## Evaluation: Performance improvement without additional computational cost; sensitivity analysis of covariance initialization (CIFAR-100/ViT-B16).

The evaluation design involves: (1) benchmark performance comparison (standard classification benchmarks), (2) sensitivity/ablation analysis on initialization. Paper [8] evaluates PEFT methods on standard benchmarks. The sensitivity analysis to initialization is a generic ablation. The benchmark family (image classification with ViT) is used in [8] and [36]. The evaluation design (standard benchmark + ablation/sensitivity) is covered by [8] and [36].

## Domain: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning / optimization for large models.

Paper [8] explicitly addresses parameter-efficient fine-tuning design spaces including LoRA. Paper [9] applies Kalman filtering to DNN optimization. The domain of PEFT for large models is clearly covered by [8].
